set.title: Picture composition · 6 more four-picture tasks
set.instruction: Four pictures tell a story. Write about 120 to 180 words. Use all four pictures, in order. Marks: 10 for content, 10 for language. Write yours first, then read the model and the note underneath it.
set.helper:
1 BEGINNING — who, where, when
2 PROBLEM — what went wrong (pictures 2 and 3)
3 ENDING — how it was solved, and how you felt

tasks.model:
Last Saturday afternoon my mother went downstairs to buy vegetables. She told me to stay in the flat and not to play ball indoors.

As soon as the door closed, I took out my football. I kicked it softly at first, then harder. On the fourth kick it flew past me and hit the blue vase on the small table. The vase wobbled, fell and broke into five pieces.

My heart was beating very fast. The vase had belonged to my grandmother. I swept the pieces into a corner with my hands and pushed them behind a box, hoping nobody would look there.

For half an hour I sat on the sofa and pretended to read. I could not read a single page.

When my mother came back, I stood up and told her everything. I said I was sorry and that I would not play ball indoors again. She was quiet for a moment. Then she put her hand on my shoulder and said that telling the truth was braver than hiding it.

We picked up the pieces together. I still feel sad about the vase, but I am glad I did not lie.
tasks.why: All four pictures are used in order, and the writer adds what the drawings cannot show: the day, the instruction not to play indoors, the fourth kick, the five pieces, the grandmother. The hiding in picture three is given real feeling — sitting on the sofa unable to read a page — instead of 'I was scared'. The ending says what the mother did and what the writer learnt, without finishing on 'I learnt my lesson'.

tasks.model:
We found her on a Tuesday, behind the canteen, where the bins are kept. She was a small brown cat and she was far too thin. You could see the shape of her bones.

My friend Devi and I were carrying our plates back. Without saying anything, we both stopped.

We put a little rice and two pieces of chicken on the ground. The cat looked at us for a long time before she came forward. Then she ate everything in less than a minute.

The next morning we came to school early. Devi brought a cardboard box from her father's shop and I brought an old towel and a plastic bowl. We put the box in the shade beside the wall and filled the bowl with water from the cooler.

By Friday the cat was sleeping in the box every afternoon. We wrote a notice and taped it to the wall: PLEASE DO NOT MOVE THE BOX. THERE IS A CAT INSIDE.

She is not thin any more. Mr Siva says she is the best mouse-catcher the canteen has ever had.
tasks.why: The pictures are followed in order, and every panel is given a detail of its own: the bins, the rice and two pieces of chicken, the box from the father's shop, the words actually written on the notice. 'You could see the shape of her bones' shows how thin she was instead of saying 'very thin'. The last two lines show the result without announcing a moral.

tasks.model:
I have lost many things at school, but never one shoe.

It was Wednesday, the day we have PE in the afternoon. I changed on the bench outside the hall as usual. When I reached into my bag for the second shoe, it was not there. Only the left one was.

I turned the whole bag upside down. I shook out my PE shirt, my water bottle and a flattened packet of biscuits. I crawled under the bench and found two bottle caps and a lot of dust. The whistle blew. I was still sitting there with one bare foot.

Then Arun came running from the other side of the hall, holding my shoe above his head like a prize. Somebody had kicked it under the far bench during recess.

I put it on in about four seconds and ran to the start line. Mr Lee let me join the second heat.

I came third out of six, which is my best result this year. The whole class clapped, and I think some of them were clapping for the shoe.
tasks.why: The search in picture two is the heart of the story, so it gets the longest paragraph and real details — the bottle caps, the dust, the whistle going while he is still sitting there. Arun holding the shoe up like a prize is one comparison, which is enough. The last line is a small joke rather than a moral, and the writer keeps the past tense throughout.

tasks.model:
Her name was Hui Shan, and she joined our class on a Monday in the middle of term, which must be the hardest time to join anything.

At recess she sat at the end of the long table by herself. She had a packet of biscuits and she was not eating them. She was reading the noticeboard on the wall, although there was nothing new on it.

I noticed because I had done the same thing in Primary 1.

I told Arun we should ask her to play catching with us. He said she might not want to. I said that was all right, but somebody still had to ask.

So we walked over and asked. She said yes so quickly that she knocked over her biscuits.

She turned out to be the fastest runner of the three of us, which Arun has still not got over.

Now we walk to the bus stop together every day. She talks the most. It is hard to believe she is the same girl who sat at the end of that table reading an empty noticeboard.
tasks.why: The writer gives a reason for noticing — 'I had done the same thing in Primary 1' — which makes the kindness believable instead of automatic. The detail of reading a noticeboard with nothing on it does the work of 'she was lonely' without saying it, and the story returns to it in the last line. Hui Shan is given something of her own: she is the fastest of the three.

tasks.model:
The second washroom on level three is the one nobody uses, because the window is broken and it is always cold in there.

I only went in because the other one had a queue.

The second tap was running hard, straight down the drain, and from the sound of it, it had been running for some time. There was nobody else in the washroom.

I tried to turn it off. The handle went round and round without tightening, and the water did not slow down at all. I tried with both hands and with the edge of my sleeve. Nothing happened except that my sleeve got wet.

So I ran. I found Uncle Raj, our cleaner, outside the library with his trolley. He listened, said "stuck washer", and came up with a spanner and a small blue toolbox.

It took him about two minutes.

The next week there was a new notice above all the basins: IF A TAP WILL NOT CLOSE, TELL AN ADULT AT ONCE. Uncle Raj says that if I had walked past, that tap would have run all weekend.
tasks.why: The opening explains why she was in an empty washroom, which a marker notices. The failed attempt is shown with specific actions — both hands, the edge of a sleeve, the wet sleeve — rather than 'I could not turn it off'. Uncle Raj gets two words of speech and a blue toolbox, which is enough to make him real. The last sentence gives the point of the story in somebody else's voice instead of the writer's.

tasks.model:
Mrs Goh lives on the eighth floor of our block. She is seventy-nine and she walks with a stick, which she does not like anybody to mention.

On Saturday morning my cousin Wei and I came back from the playground and found her standing in front of the lift with two shopping bags on the floor beside her. One was full of tins.

Then we saw the notice taped to the lift door: LIFT UNDER REPAIR UNTIL 2 P.M.

It was half past ten.

She said she would wait. We said we would carry the bags up for her, and after she had said no twice, she said all right.

The bag of tins was heavier than my school bag with every book in it. We changed hands at the fourth floor and again at the sixth. Mrs Goh came up slowly behind us, one step at a time, and told us to stop and rest whenever we liked.

At her door she went inside and came out with a tin of pineapple tarts, the good kind in the gold tin.

We were not expecting anything. But I will not pretend we were sorry about the tarts.
tasks.why: Mrs Goh is made a person in two lines, including something she does not like mentioned — the sort of detail that lifts content marks. Refusing twice before accepting is true to life. The weight is shown by comparison with a full school bag, and by changing hands at named floors. The ending is honest and a little funny instead of 'I felt happy because I had helped somebody'.
